summary: A 1970 note describing a prototype implementation of the Network Control Program (NCP), the host software handling network communication. It was written by members of the UCLA group.

eli5.summary: This is a first try at building the program that lets a computer talk on the network, like a rough prototype before the real thing.

questions: how did ncp flow control work
subtitle: A worked example, in prose, of how a host's Network Control Program could be built.

tldr.problem: Sites had to write their own Network Control Programs (NCPs) for very different systems, and the formal protocol in RFC 54 alone did not show how the pieces fit together.
tldr.mechanism: The authors describe a prototype NCP for an imagined time-sharing host: system calls, five component programs, eight tables, narratives of opening, flow control and closing, and a ten-state connection diagram.
tldr.outcome: It is explicitly an example and not a model. Nothing in it must be implemented, and only the rules in RFC 54 are binding.

today: RFC 55 is an early example description with status Unknown and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states itself that it is only an example, so it is not a specification.

sections.title: Why a Prototype NCP
sections.content:
J. Newkirk and M. Kraley of Harvard and J. Postel and S. Crocker of UCLA tried to write a prototypical NCP in an Algol-like language. After some weeks the project was abandoned because the code was becoming unreadable, so they wrote it as prose instead.

They say there is absolutely no requirement to implement anything in the document. The only rigid rules an NCP must follow are in RFC 54, and this description is an example, not a model. They assume a time-sharing host where processes own ports, each port is tied one-to-one to a socket, and a process is not put to sleep when it tries to LISTEN or CONNECT.
sections.eli5: They tried writing the program as code, but it got messy, so they explained it in words. It is only a sample, not a rule.

sections.title: System Calls, Programs and Tables
sections.content:
The example system calls are CONNECT, LISTEN, ACCEPT, TRANSMIT, INT, STATUS and CLOSE. Each returns a condition code such as OK, BUSY, BADSKT or NOROOM, and a process can look at a port's status at any time with STATUS.

The NCP has five component programs: an Input Handler and an Output Handler (both interrupt-driven), an Input Interpreter, an Output Scheduler and a System Call Interpreter. The scheduler gives priority to Host-to-Imp messages, then control messages, then regular messages.

The main data lives in associative tables: the Rendezvous Table, which holds the attributes of a connection, the Input Link Table, the Output Link Table, the Port Table, the Output Control Command Table, the Output Request Queue, the Host Live Table and the Link Assignment Table. The Host Live Table notes that the protocol does not yet define host up and host down handling and points to RFC 57.
sections.eli5: The design has a few helpers, one for listening, one for sending, one for deciding what messages mean, and some notebooks to remember who is talking to whom.

sections.title: Opening, Flow Control and Closing
sections.content:
Opening a connection takes a pair of RFCs (generic for RTS and STR): an RTS from the receive side with a link number, and an STR from the send side. Pending calls must be queued, since the network is asynchronous and a request may arrive before the LISTEN. When a CONNECT is issued, the NCP refuses non-matching pending requests by sending CLS.

For flow control, a cell called 'Their Size' starts at zero. The receive side sends ALL messages that add buffer space (increments, not absolute sizes), the sender subtracts each message length, and it cannot send when the value is zero. The length field of ALL can be 32 bits long.

Closing needs two CLS commands, just as opening needs two RFCs. The text separates aborting, refusing, termination by the receiver and termination by the sender. A sender must wait for its buffer to empty and for the RFNM before sending CLS.
sections.eli5: To start talking both sides say yes. The listener tells the speaker how much it can hold, and to hang up both say goodbye.

sections.title: The Ten Connection States
sections.content:
Each socket is described by a state machine with ten states, shown in Figure 7.1 of the RFC. Network events move a socket between states, some events are ignored and others are errors.

The remainder of the RFC gives algorithms for the Input Interpreter, covering NOP, RFC, CLS, ERR, ECO, ERP, INR, INS, ALL and Data-RFNM, and for the System Call Interpreter, covering CONNECT, LISTEN, ACCEPT and the other calls.
sections.eli5: A connection is always in one of ten moods, like waiting, open or closing, and each message moves it to the next mood.

items.label: CLOSED
items.desc: Socket not attached to a port and no connection requested.

items.label: PENDING CALL
items.desc: Connection requests received but no port attached.

items.label: LISTENING
items.desc: Attached to a port, waiting for a caller.

items.label: RFC-RCVD
items.desc: An RFC arrived; the user must ACCEPT or CLOSE.

items.label: ABORT
items.desc: Foreign user aborted before the local user responded.

items.label: RFC-SENT
items.desc: A CONNECT was issued and no reply has come.

items.label: OPEN
items.desc: RFCs exchanged; data may flow under flow control.

items.label: DATA-WAIT
items.desc: Send side waiting for buffer to empty and RFNM.

items.label: RFNM-WAIT
items.desc: Waiting for the last RFNM before closing.

references.text: NWG/RFC 54, the protocol rules an NCP must follow.
Kraley, M., Newkirk, J., "Thoughts and Reflections on NWG/RFC #54", RFC 57, June 1970.
